name: Agreement with the Sisseton and Wahpeton of 1889, ratified by the Act of March 3, 1891 (Lake Traverse surplus lands, Royce 496)
citation: Act of March 3, 1891, ch. 543, 26 Stat. 989, 1035 (agreement of December 12, 1889; section 27 at 1038)
promises: Article 1: the bands ceded all unallotted land of the Lake Traverse Reservation left after allotments (DeCoteau, quoting the agreement).
Article 2: the United States would pay $2.50 an acre for the ceded land.
Article 3: back annuities would be paid and the annuities of $18,400 continued to July 1, 1901.
Article 4: allotments would be equalised so that each person, married women included, had 160 acres.

Section 27 of the ratifying Act: the purchase money would be held in the Treasury in trust for the bands at 5 percent interest (the agreement had said 3), to be used for their education and civilization (ICC Docket 363, 1975).

breaches.what: In the bands' accounting claim the Commission held that the United States kept part of the fund from this cession (the minors' shares) at 3 percent instead of the 5 percent section 27 required, calling that fund established illegally, and surcharged it with the shortfall and with $358.76 and $1,236.26 it had carried to surplus. It also disallowed a 1919 transfer of $313.09 from the fund's interest that the United States admitted was improper.

breaches.what: Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate Chairman Dave Flute writes that Congress let the 1867 treaty be renegotiated by ratifying an agreement opening the reservation to homesteaders, which cost the tribe 678,778 acres, and that the tribe rejects treaty renegotiation.

source.title: 'We have always been a very proud people': Dave Flute on tribes and treaties (June 5, 2018)

landTaken: The Senate report quoted in DeCoteau estimated the surplus at 678,778 acres; the Court of Claims gives the final surplus as 608,865.56 acres.
compensation: $2.50 an acre. Congress appropriated $2,203,000 for the land and the loyal scout claim (DeCoteau). After allotments the surplus proved smaller than estimated, and $236,048.83 was deducted (58 Ct. Cl. 302). The Commission in 1975 accepted the 1898 return of $177,635.85 to the Treasury as the price of the 71,055 acres overestimated in 1891 (679,950 estimated, 608,865 actual), plus $58,412.88 of interest (Docket 363).
today: In 1923 the Court of Claims dismissed the bands' claims, including one for the $236,048.83 deduction, for lack of proof (58 Ct. Cl. 302). In DeCoteau v. District County Court (1975) the Supreme Court held that the 1891 Act terminated the Lake Traverse Reservation, a ruling against the tribe. The 1975 Commission surcharges in Docket 363 were part of an accounting still open in 1975; a final judgment on them was not traced.

nationVoice.summary: Its chairman wrote in 2018 that Congress allowed the 1867 treaty to be renegotiated when it opened the reservation to homesteaders, costing 678,778 acres, and that the Oyate rejects treaty renegotiation.

openQuestions: Audit 2026-11-08 (round 14): Dockets 142 and 359 to 363 read. Their land claims (the Minnesota treaties of 1851 and later) were compromised for $12,250,000 in 1967 (18 Ind. Cl. Comm. 477) and do not include this cession. The general accounting claim in Docket 363 was kept out of that settlement; its 1975 opinion (36 Ind. Cl. Comm. 295) rules on the trust fund from this cession and is added as a claims-commission breach, raising the status from contested to broken. No finding that the $2.50 price was unconscionable was found.

The 1923 deduction of $236,048.83 (58 Ct. Cl. 302) is $0.10 more than the two transfers the Commission describes, $177,635.85 of principal and $58,412.88 of interest (sum computed for this file). Not reconciled.

The sums surcharged in 1975 are small: the 2 percent shortfall on the minors' fund was ordered computed, not stated, and the total recovered was not traced. Whether Docket 363 ended in a judgment, a settlement or a transfer to the Court of Claims in 1978 was not traced.
Royce's link in treaties.json points to p. 842 (the 1867 treaty); the 1891 entry is on p. 942.
The Oyate's own website (swo-nsn.gov) had no history page on the 1891 Act that loaded; the chairman's 2018 article is used instead.

plain.promised: The bands sold the unallotted Lake Traverse land for $2.50 an acre, with 160 acres for every member, and the money was to be held in trust for them at 5 percent interest.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1975 that the United States paid only 3 percent on part of that trust money and wrongly moved small sums out of it. The Oyate says the Act cost it 678,778 acres.
plain.today: The 1975 sums were small and their final payment was not traced. A 1923 claim was dismissed, and in 1975 the Supreme Court held the Act ended the reservation, a ruling against the tribe.
